## Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Explain why **data alone cannot always determine the direction of a causal arrow**
- Describe what structure-learning algorithms **can do** (narrow possibilities) and what they **cannot** (guarantee the right arrows)
- Combine **expert knowledge** with algorithmic output to build stronger causal models
- Describe the **feedback loop** between data and causal models — each improves the other
- Use `bnlearn::hc()` in R to **learn a DAG from simulated data** and compare it to the truth
:::

**The final chapter:** Throughout Chapters 1--9, we drew the arrows ourselves based on expert knowledge. This chapter asks: **Can a computer figure out the arrows just from data?** The answer is nuanced — and that nuance is the most important lesson in the course.
:::


# The Big Question {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Can data discover causes?</span>


## Can the Computer Draw the Arrows?

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**What we have been doing (Chapters 1--9)**

- An expert draws the DAG based on domain knowledge
- We assign numbers from data or expert judgment
- We use the DAG for inference, decisions, and resource allocation

*The DAG came from human expertise.*
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**The new question (Chapter 10)**

- We have a dataset with many variables
- Can a computer algorithm figure out which arrows to draw?
- Can it tell us what causes what — just from patterns in the data?

*Can the DAG come from the data itself?*
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Spoiler alert:** The answer is *partly* yes and *partly* no. Data can narrow down the possibilities dramatically — but it cannot always determine the direction of every arrow. That is why **you** still matter.
:::


# Same Pattern, Different Arrows {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Why data alone is not enough</span>


## Three Simple DAGs

Consider three variables — **Staffing (S)**, **Training (T)**, and **Mortality (M)** — and three ways the arrows could go:

<div style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.7em; margin: 0.6em 0;">
<table style="width: 90%; margin: 0 auto;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em; border: 2px solid #005CB9; border-radius: 8px;">
<strong>DAG 1: Chain</strong><br>
<span class="dag-node treatment">S</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">→</span>
<span class="dag-node confounder">T</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">→</span>
<span class="dag-node outcome">M</span><br>
<span style="font-size: 0.85em;">"Staffing drives Training,<br>which drives Mortality"</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em; border: 2px solid #83BD00; border-radius: 8px;">
<strong>DAG 2: Fork</strong><br>
<span class="dag-node treatment">S</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">←</span>
<span class="dag-node confounder">T</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">→</span>
<span class="dag-node outcome">M</span><br>
<span style="font-size: 0.85em;">"Training drives both<br>Staffing and Mortality"</span>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em; border: 2px solid #F8A623; border-radius: 8px;">
<strong>DAG 3: Reverse Chain</strong><br>
<span class="dag-node treatment">S</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">←</span>
<span class="dag-node confounder">T</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">←</span>
<span class="dag-node outcome">M</span><br>
<span style="font-size: 0.85em;">"Mortality drives Training,<br>which drives Staffing"</span>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**The surprising fact:** All three DAGs produce the *same* statistical pattern in the data. If you know T, then S and M become independent. No amount of data can tell you which of these three is correct.
:::


## The Collider Is the Exception

Now look at a fourth arrangement:

<div style="text-align: center; margin: 0.6em 0;">
<table style="width: 40%; margin: 0 auto;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em; border: 2px solid #E24A3F; border-radius: 8px;">
<strong>DAG 4: Collider</strong><br>
<span class="dag-node treatment">S</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">→</span>
<span class="dag-node confounder">T</span>
<span class="dag-arrow">←</span>
<span class="dag-node outcome">M</span><br>
<span style="font-size: 0.85em;">"Both Staffing and Mortality<br>independently drive Training"</span>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

. . .

This one is **different**. In the collider:

- S and M are independent when you do NOT know T
- S and M become *dependent* when you DO know T
- This is the opposite pattern from the chain and fork

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Key insight:** The collider creates a unique data fingerprint. If the algorithm detects this pattern, it can determine the arrow direction. Colliders are the one structure that data *can* identify on its own.
:::


## The Core Problem: A Summary

<div style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.65em; margin: 0.5em 0;">
<table style="width: 95%; margin: 0 auto; border-collapse: separate; border-spacing: 0.5em;">
<tr>
<th style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;">Data Pattern</th>
<th style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;">Compatible DAGs</th>
<th style="text-align: center; padding: 0.5em;">Can Data Decide?</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px;">S and M independent given T</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px;">S→T→M &nbsp; S←T→M &nbsp; S←T←M</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px; color: #E24A3F; font-weight: 700;">No — 3 options remain</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px;">S and M independent, but dependent given T</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px;">S→T←M</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 4px; color: #83BD00; font-weight: 700;">Yes — only 1 option</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

. . .

::: {.definition-box}
**The bottom line:** When two different DAGs produce the same data pattern, they are called **Markov equivalent**. No statistical test — no matter how large the sample — can distinguish between them. Only expert knowledge or experimental data can break the tie.
:::


# What Algorithms Can Do {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Narrowing down the possibilities</span>


## From Millions of Options to a Handful

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .red}
**Without an algorithm:**

With just 5 variables, there are **29,281** possible DAGs. With 10 variables, the number exceeds **4 trillion**. You could never check them all by hand.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**With an algorithm:**

The algorithm tests which variables are connected and which are independent. It eliminates the vast majority. You end up with a small set of DAGs — often just a handful — consistent with the data.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**Think of it like a detective.** The algorithm cannot always name the one culprit. But it can narrow the suspect list from thousands down to three or four. That is enormously helpful.
:::


## How the Algorithm Works (Intuition)

You do not need to know the math. Here is the basic idea behind **score-based** structure learning:

. . .

<div class="step-flow">
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #005CB9;"><strong>Step 1</strong><br>Start with<br>no arrows</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #83BD00;"><strong>Step 2</strong><br>Try adding<br>an arrow</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #F8A623;"><strong>Step 3</strong><br>Does the DAG<br>fit better?</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #FA7650;"><strong>Step 4</strong><br>Keep if yes,<br>discard if no</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #3E9B6E;"><strong>Step 5</strong><br>Repeat until<br>no improvement</div>
</div>

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**The scoring function** balances two things: how well the DAG explains the data (fit) versus how many arrows it uses (simplicity). The algorithm finds the sweet spot. This is called **hill climbing** — the approach behind `bnlearn::hc()`.
:::


# What Algorithms Cannot Do {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">The limits of data-driven discovery</span>


## Three Limitations

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**1. Arrow direction (usually)**

When two variables are correlated, the algorithm often cannot tell whether A causes B or B causes A. The chain and the reverse chain look identical in the data.

. . .

**2. Hidden variables**

If a confounder is not in your dataset, the algorithm cannot find it. It might draw a direct arrow between two variables that are actually both caused by something unmeasured.
:::

::: {.col}
**3. The "why"**

The algorithm tells you that Staffing and NMR are connected. It does not tell you *why* — whether it is because better-staffed facilities provide better emergency care, or because staffing is a proxy for overall facility quality.

. . .

::: {.callout-box .red}
**A learned DAG is a hypothesis, not a proof.** It tells you what the data is *consistent with*. It does not tell you what is *true*.
:::
:::
:::


## When Direction Is Ambiguous

Imagine the algorithm finds that **Training** and **Quality of Care** are strongly associated. It says: "These two are connected." But which arrow is correct?

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**Option A:** Training → Quality

Training improves quality. This is the intuitive story — you invest in training *because* you believe it improves care.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Option B:** Quality → Training

High-quality facilities attract more training opportunities. They have the reputation and infrastructure that training programs seek out.
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**How do you break the tie?** You ask someone who knows the health system. A clinician would tell you: "Training came first — the facilities received training, and *then* quality improved." Expert knowledge resolves the ambiguity that data alone cannot.
:::


# The Best Approach: Expert + Algorithm {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Why humans and computers work better together</span>


## The Partnership

<div style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.6em; margin: 0.5em 0;">
<table style="width: 95%; margin: 0 auto;">
<tr><th style="padding: 0.5em;">Approach</th><th style="padding: 0.5em;">Strengths</th><th style="padding: 0.5em;">Weaknesses</th></tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;"><strong>Expert only</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;">Understands mechanisms, temporal order, context</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;">May miss unexpected connections; biased by prior beliefs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;"><strong>Algorithm only</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;">Checks every possible connection; finds surprises</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd;">Cannot determine all arrow directions; blind to unmeasured variables</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; background-color: rgba(131, 189, 0, 0.1);"><strong>Expert + Algorithm</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; background-color: rgba(131, 189, 0, 0.1);">Human draws DAG; computer checks data; disagreements trigger investigation</td>
<td style="padding: 0.5em; border: 1px solid #ddd; background-color: rgba(131, 189, 0, 0.1);">Requires both expertise and data — but that is what good research looks like</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

. . .

::: {.key-takeaway}
**The winning strategy:** You draw the DAG from what you know. The computer checks if the data agrees. Where they disagree, you investigate. This is how science actually works — theory and evidence in conversation.
:::


## The Three-Step Workflow

<div class="step-flow">
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #005CB9;"><strong>Step 1: Draw</strong><br>Expert draws DAG<br>from domain knowledge</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #83BD00;"><strong>Step 2: Learn</strong><br>Algorithm learns DAG<br>from data</div>
<div class="step-arrow">→</div>
<div class="step-item" style="border-left: 4px solid #E24A3F;"><strong>Step 3: Compare</strong><br>Where do they agree?<br>Where do they disagree?</div>
</div>

. . .

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**Where they agree:** High confidence. Both theory and data point the same way. Trust the arrow.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .orange}
**Where they disagree:** Investigate. Maybe the expert was wrong. Maybe the data is misleading. Maybe there is a hidden variable. This is where the most interesting discoveries happen.
:::
:::
:::


# The Feedback Loop {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Data refines model, model guides data</span>


## The Virtuous Cycle

Here is the big-picture conclusion of the entire course:

<div style="text-align: center; margin: 1em 0;">
<table style="margin: 0 auto; border-collapse: separate; border-spacing: 0.3em; font-size: 0.6em;">
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em;">
<div class="dag-node decision rect" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em; font-size: 1.1em;">Expert<br>Knowledge</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.8em;">→</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em; font-size: 1.1em;">Causal<br>Model</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.8em;">→</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em; font-size: 1.1em; border-color: #83BD00; color: #83BD00;">Testable<br>Predictions</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.2em;">↑</td>
<td></td>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.2em;">↓</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em; font-size: 1.1em; border-color: #F8A623; color: #F8A623;">Revised<br>Understanding</div>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.8em;">←</td>
<td style="text-align: center; padding: 0.8em;">
<div class="dag-node" style="padding: 0.5em 0.8em; font-size: 1.1em; border-color: #E24A3F; color: #E24A3F;">Data<br>Collection</div>
</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**The cycle never truly ends.** You start with knowledge, build a model, make predictions, collect data, check the predictions, revise the model, and start again. Each pass makes your understanding sharper and your decisions better.
:::


## What Each Step Does

::: {.incremental}
1. **Expert Knowledge → Causal Model:** Draw the DAG based on what you know (Chapters 1--3)
2. **Causal Model → Testable Predictions:** The DAG implies statistical patterns — "If my DAG is right, X and Y should be independent given Z" (Chapters 4--6)
3. **Testable Predictions → Data Collection:** You know exactly what to measure and look for (Chapters 7--8)
4. **Data Collection → Revised Understanding:** Data confirms your predictions (good!) or surprises you (even better — you learn something new)
5. **Revised Understanding → Expert Knowledge:** Update your DAG and start the next cycle stronger
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**This is the scientific method applied to causal modeling.** It is not a one-time exercise. It is a living process that gets better with every iteration.
:::


# MNH Application: Tanzania's Health Data {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Using real health information systems to check our models</span>


## Tanzania's Digital Health Infrastructure

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**DHIS2 & GoTHOMIS:**

- **DHIS2** (District Health Information System 2) covers routine health data at approximately **80% of health facilities**
- **GoTHOMIS** handles individual-level clinical records
- Together, they capture staffing, equipment, service delivery, and outcomes
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**What this means for us:**

Tanzania has the *data infrastructure* to test causal models against real facility-level records.

When we draw a DAG predicting that staffing affects delivery outcomes, we can check: **Does the DHIS2 data agree?**

This is the feedback loop in action.
:::
:::
:::


## Testing Predictions with Facility Data

::: {.example-block}
[MNH Example]{.example-label}

**Expert prediction:** "Adequate staffing reduces neonatal mortality, partly through improved emergency response capability."

**The DAG says:** Staffing → Emergency Response → NMR. This implies that if you know Emergency Response, Staffing and NMR should become less correlated.

**The data test:** Using DHIS2 facility records, check whether the correlation between staffing and neonatal outcomes weakens after controlling for emergency C-section rates (a proxy for emergency response).

**If the data agrees:** Confidence in the DAG goes up.

**If the data disagrees:** Maybe staffing also has a direct effect through other pathways. Revise the DAG.
:::


## What We Can Discover

With large-scale DHIS2 data from Tanzanian facilities, a structure-learning algorithm might discover:

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **Expected connections:** Staffing and outcomes are linked (algorithm confirms what experts believe)
- **Surprising connections:** Drug stock-outs are more strongly linked to mortality than equipment availability — suggesting supply chain might matter more than capital investment
- **Missing connections:** Training completion does not directly predict outcomes — maybe the link works only through on-the-job practice
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Each surprise is a gift.** The algorithm did not prove the expert wrong — it pointed to exactly where the expert should look more carefully.
:::


# R Workshop: Structure Learning {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">Learning a DAG from simulated data with bnlearn</span>


## R Block 1: Simulate Health Facility Data

We create a simulated dataset mimicking DHIS2 data. We know the "true" DAG — so we can see how well the algorithm does.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-data
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(bnlearn)

set.seed(42)
n <- 1000  # Simulated facilities

# ── The "TRUE" causal structure (known to us, hidden from the algorithm) ──
# Training → Staffing → NMR;  DrugAvail → NMR
# Equipment → Referral;  Staffing → Referral

training    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.6)
drug_avail  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.7)
equipment   <- rnorm(n, 0.5, 0.15) |> pmin(1) |> pmax(0)
staffing    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.35 * training)
referral    <- 20 - 5 * staffing - 4 * equipment + rnorm(n, 0, 3)
nmr         <- 30 - 6 * staffing - 4 * drug_avail + rnorm(n, 0, 5)

facility_data <- data.frame(
  Training = training, DrugAvail = drug_avail, Equipment = equipment,
  Staffing = staffing, Referral = referral, NMR = nmr
)

cat("Dataset:", n, "facilities,", ncol(facility_data), "variables\n")
head(facility_data)
```

::: {.callout-box}
**What we built:** A 5-arrow DAG with 6 variables. The algorithm does not know the true structure — it only sees the data.
:::


## R Block 2: Learn the DAG and Compare

```{r}
#| label: learn-and-compare
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Define the TRUE DAG for comparison
true_dag <- model2network(
 "[Training][DrugAvail][Equipment][Staffing|Training][Referral|Staffing:Equipment][NMR|Staffing:DrugAvail]"
)

# Hill Climbing: tries adding, removing, reversing arrows
# Keeps changes that improve the score
learned_dag <- hc(facility_data)

# ── Compare: which arrows did the algorithm get right? ──
true_arcs    <- arcs(true_dag)
learned_arcs <- arcs(learned_dag)
correct      <- merge(true_arcs, learned_arcs)

cat("True DAG arrows:", nrow(true_arcs), "\n")
cat("Learned DAG arrows:", nrow(learned_arcs), "\n")
cat("Correct arrows:", nrow(correct), "out of", nrow(true_arcs), "\n")

# What did it miss or add?
missed <- true_arcs[!paste(true_arcs[,1], true_arcs[,2]) %in%
                     paste(learned_arcs[,1], learned_arcs[,2]), ]
extra  <- learned_arcs[!paste(learned_arcs[,1], learned_arcs[,2]) %in%
                        paste(true_arcs[,1], true_arcs[,2]), ]

cat("\nMissed arrows:\n"); print(missed)
cat("\nExtra arrows (false positives):\n"); print(extra)
```


## R Block 3: Visualize the Comparison

```{r}
#| label: visualize-comparison
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Side-by-side: True DAG vs. Learned DAG
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

graphviz.plot(true_dag,
              main = "True DAG (what we built)",
              shape = "ellipse",
              highlight = list(nodes = "NMR",
                               fill = "#E24A3F", col = "#E24A3F"))

graphviz.plot(learned_dag,
              main = "Learned DAG (what the algorithm found)",
              shape = "ellipse",
              highlight = list(nodes = "NMR",
                               fill = "#E24A3F", col = "#E24A3F"))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-box .green}
**Typical result with 1,000 observations:** The algorithm gets **4 out of 5 arrows correct**. It finds all the right connections but may reverse one arrow direction. That reversed arrow is exactly where expert knowledge steps in.
:::


## Interpreting the Results

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**What the algorithm typically gets right:**

- The **connections** (skeleton) — which variables are linked
- **Collider structures** — where two arrows point in
- Strong effects with large sample sizes

**What it typically gets wrong:**

- **Arrow direction** in chains — it may flip an arrow
- Weak effects — small effects may be missed entirely
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box}
**The expert's role:**

When the algorithm says "Training and Staffing are connected," you ask: "Which came first?"

Training programs are *deployed* to improve staffing. Staffing does not create training programs.

**Temporal order resolves the ambiguity.** The arrow must go Training → Staffing.
:::

::: {.callout-box .green}
**This is the Expert + Algorithm partnership.** The algorithm found the connection. The expert determined the direction. Together, they are stronger than either alone.
:::
:::
:::


# Course Summary {background-color="#005CB9"}

<span style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.7); font-size: 0.7em;">The 10-chapter journey</span>


## The Four Pillars of the Course

<div class="step-flow">

## The Complete Toolkit

::: {.columns-equal}
::: {.col}
**What you can now do:**

1. **Draw a causal model** from expert knowledge (Ch 1--3)
2. **Add probabilities** from data or expert estimates (Ch 4--5)
3. **Avoid reasoning traps** — confounding, selection bias, collider bias (Ch 1, 6)
4. **Calculate the value** of different interventions (Ch 7)
5. **Allocate resources** optimally across competing options (Ch 8)
6. **Anticipate strategic responses** from other actors (Ch 9)
7. **Check your model against data** and refine it (Ch 10)
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.callout-box .green}
**The MNH analyst's workflow:**

1. Interview experts, draw the DAG (Ch 2--3)
2. Populate it with DHIS2 data (Ch 4--5, 10)
3. Identify the best intervention targets (Ch 7)
4. Allocate resources across countries (Ch 8)
5. Design incentive-compatible contracts (Ch 9)
6. Collect new data, check predictions, refine (Ch 10)

**This is not a one-time analysis. It is a continuous cycle of learning and improving.**
:::
:::
:::


## Key Takeaways

::: {.key-takeaway}
**Structure Learning from Observational Data**

1. **Data alone cannot always determine causation.** Different causal structures can produce the same data pattern. Only colliders create a unique fingerprint that data can identify.

2. **Algorithms narrow down the possibilities dramatically.** From trillions of possible DAGs, the algorithm finds the handful consistent with the data. That is powerful — even if it cannot pick the single right one.

3. **Expert knowledge + algorithm = best answer.** The algorithm finds connections; the expert determines direction. This partnership is stronger than either approach alone.

4. **The feedback loop is the course's central insight.** Data refines your causal model. The model tells you what data to collect next. Each cycle makes your understanding — and your decisions — better.
:::


## Congratulations

You have completed **Inference and Intervention**.

. . .

::: {.definition-box}
**The central message of the course:**

Causal models are not just academic diagrams. They are **practical tools** for answering the questions that matter most: *Where should we invest? What will happen if we do? How do we know we are right?*

The combination of **qualitative modeling**, **quantitative analysis**, **decision theory**, and **data-driven discovery** provides a complete framework for making better decisions under uncertainty.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-box}
**The most important thing you take away** is not any single technique. It is a way of thinking: *always ask what causes what, draw it out, check it against evidence, and be willing to revise when the evidence says you were wrong.*

That is what separates good analysis from great analysis. And great analysis saves lives.
:::
